summary: Diameter nodes have no generic way to know the relative priority of messages when they make routing and resource allocation decisions. This proposed standard defines a mechanism that lets Diameter endpoints indicate the priority of a transaction. Nodes can then use it, for example, when they are overloaded.

eli5.summary: At a busy airport, emergency flights should land first. This lets messages in a network-login system carry a priority label so the important ones get handled first when things get busy.

questions: what is diameter routing message priority
what is the default drmp priority
subtitle: A priority label for Diameter messages, so busy networks throttle the least important requests first.

tldr.problem: When Diameter nodes are overloaded and must throttle requests, they have no generic way to tell which requests matter more, so every request is equally likely to be dropped.
tldr.mechanism: The Diameter Routing Message Priority (DRMP) AVP, code 301, carries a priority from 0 (highest) to 15 (lowest) in requests and optionally answers, and nodes MAY use it for routing, throttling and resource decisions.
tldr.outcome: Agents can protect important traffic such as first-responder signaling without understanding each application, but the scheme only works inside a trusted, consistently configured domain.

today: RFC 7944 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the overload control work in RFC 7683 and the base protocol in RFC 6733.

sections.title: The Problem: All Requests Look Alike
sections.content:
The Diameter Overload Indication Conveyance (DOIC) solution, RFC 7683, lets overloaded Diameter nodes ask others to send less traffic. Clients and agents then throttle requests, which means permanently rejecting some transactions.

With the mechanisms available before this RFC, nodes cannot tell requests apart when they choose what to throttle. All requests have the same probability of being throttled. The RFC notes that application-specific priority AVPs exist, but using them would force agents to understand every application and parse every message, which it calls an unacceptable level of complexity for elements whose job is to route.

RFC 7944 defines a generic priority marking that agents can read without any application knowledge. Its main use is throttling input, but it may also feed route selection and endpoint resource allocation.
sections.eli5: If a teacher sends home every kid at once when the school is too crowded, nobody gets to choose who stays. A priority sticker lets the school keep the most important kids first.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC lists four situations where marking priority helps.

  • First responders. After a natural disaster, load rises and capacity may fall, so overload control kicks in. First-responder signaling needs higher priority. The text names the US Wireless Priority Services (WPS) and Government Emergency Telecommunications Service (GETS) as examples of systems for these needs.
  • Emergency calls. Their signaling should also get preferential treatment when possible.
  • Differentiated services. An operator might sell Platinum, Gold and Silver service level agreements and mark Platinum customers' signaling as higher priority.
  • Application-specific priorities. Later steps in a multi-step access procedure, or session updates and endings, might be marked above session starts, because more work is already invested. One example is a 3GPP S6a Update Location Request caused by Mobility Management Entity restoration, which might outrank one from an initial attach.
sections.eli5: Ambulances get to go through red lights, and a ticket that says VIP gets you in faster. Different reasons, but each gets a higher spot in line.

sections.title: Theory of Operation
sections.content:
Behavior depends on the role a node plays in a transaction.

  1. Request sender decides the priority (how is application specific and out of scope), puts it in the request and saves it with the transaction state.
  2. Agents use it to decide which requests to route first, which to throttle and where to send them. Agents generally neither change nor add priority. In exceptional cases an edge agent may rewrite values set by an adjacent operator, or insert a priority for an endpoint that does not support DRMP. Agents also save the priority, either locally or in Proxy-Info from RFC 6733.
  3. Request handler can use it to order work and allocate resources.
  4. Answer sender uses the request's priority for the answer, and may include its own DRMP AVP if the answer needs a different priority.
  5. Agents and the answer handler use the stored priority by default, but a priority carried in the answer replaces it.
sections.eli5: The sender puts a sticker on a parcel, the post offices along the way sort by the sticker, and the reply parcel usually gets the same sticker unless the receiver picks a new one.

sections.title: The DRMP AVP and Its Values
sections.content:
The DRMP AVP has AVP code 301 and type Enumerated. Its value is one of PRIORITY_0 to PRIORITY_15, with numbers 0 to 15. The scale runs backwards from what many people expect: PRIORITY_0 is the highest priority and PRIORITY_15 is the lowest. Formally, PRIORITY_x is lower priority than PRIORITY_y when y is less than x.

The AVP flag rules say the V bit MUST NOT be set. New AVP codes come from the AAA Parameters registry, in its AVP Codes subregistry, per the IANA section.
sections.eli5: It is like a race where the person who gets number 0 goes first and number 15 goes last. Smaller number, more important.

sections.title: Normative Behavior and Defaults
sections.content:
When priority information is available, Diameter nodes SHOULD put the DRMP AVP in all request messages. Nodes SHOULD use it, when present, for overload throttling decisions. Agents MAY use it when relaying requests and answers, for route selection and message ordering. Endpoints MAY use it for resource allocation, and MAY include a DRMP AVP in answers.

For answers, nodes SHOULD use the priority in the answer's DRMP AVP if there is one, and otherwise the request's priority.

Every node MUST have a default priority for transactions with no DRMP AVP. To treat non-upgraded clients consistently, nodes SHOULD use PRIORITY_10, a midrange value for normal traffic. Nodes MUST let operators change the default through local configuration. Applying the default does not mean an agent inserts a DRMP AVP; the message is only treated as if it had one.
sections.eli5: If a parcel has no sticker, the post office treats it as a normal one, number 10. The boss can change what counts as normal, but nobody sticks new labels on just for that.

sections.title: Applicability and Defining Priorities
sections.content:
Two things must hold for DRMP to work well. First, priorities for all messages across all applications in one administrative domain must be defined in a consistent, coordinated way, otherwise one application's messages can gain unwarranted preferential treatment. This does not matter if every node supports just one application. Second, DRMP AVPs must be inserted by trusted nodes. When messages cross administrative boundaries, care should be taken to strip or modify the values.

The RFC adds design cautions. Higher-priority messages can block lower-priority ones, which are often retried and can produce more traffic than without DRMP; it suggests keeping high-priority traffic a small share normally, though blocking is a requirement in cases such as first-responder messages. The same values should be used across applications for the same use case. For illustration only, it suggests PRIORITY_2 for first responders and PRIORITY_3 for emergency calls. Messages from non-upgraded clients or with stripped AVPs get the default, and the rollout process can cause similar messages to be treated differently.
sections.eli5: Everyone in the whole school has to agree what a gold star means. If one class hands out gold stars for everything, its kids cut in line unfairly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A malicious node could insert artificially high priorities to gain preferential treatment, and a malicious or compromised agent could change a sender's priority up or down. Diameter has no end-to-end authentication, integrity protection or confidentiality, and transport security (TLS, DTLS or IPsec) protects only between peers, so agents can read and modify the DRMP AVP. Trust is therefore transitive along the path.

If DRMP only feeds overload throttling, attacks matter mainly while nodes are overloaded. If it affects message ordering, the impact applies at all times. The RFC says DRMP opens no direct denial-of-service vector, but a rogue agent can degrade a node's service.

Nodes supporting DRMP MUST let operators choose which peers are trusted to deliver DRMP AVPs, and whether those peers are trusted to forward them from non-adjacent nodes. Nodes MUST strip DRMP AVPs from messages received from peers not trusted for DRMP.
sections.eli5: If anyone can write VIP on their own ticket, everyone will. So the school only trusts stickers from people it already knows, and peels off the rest.

messages.label: Request + DRMP
messages.note: Sender sets priority and saves it with the transaction state.

messages.label: Request + DRMP
messages.note: Agent routes or throttles using the priority, and saves it.

messages.label: Answer (DRMP optional)
messages.note: Request priority applies unless the answer carries its own.

messages.label: Answer
messages.note: Stored priority is used unless the answer has a DRMP AVP.
